text: some personal news: Byro got accepted into TooEarly Ventures validation programme. finally, “you're too early” came with a welcome email. there are five of us now, building an AI head of content for B2B teams. we want to help teams turn the knowledge inside their company into content without making everyone take on a second job in marketing. the next step is getting closer to the people we're building for. understanding what fits into their working week, what saves them time, and what we've made unnecessarily complicated. i suspect that last category will be humbling. excited to work through it with the TooEarly team. thank you for having us. W's in the chat

Byro is now five people. looking for six and seven. specifically: someone technical who likes building and shipping software. someone in marketing who can turn a good idea into something people actually notice. we're building an AI head of content for B2B teams, helping turn company expertise into content that drives revenue. there's plenty to build, test, break, fix, and tell people about. open to internships too. if you're early in your career, show us something you've made, a project you've worked on, or an idea you couldn't leave alone. message me with what you'd like to work on, your availability, and something you're proud of. or send this to the person you'd immediately want on your own team. five people in. two seats open. still early enough to have strong opinions about the whole thing

our fake funding announcement brought Byro real users. 4,200 likes. 1,000 new followers. teams from our 'potential users' slide actually signing up. someone even sent us €100. we've retrospectively decided this was a marketing strategy.

some personal news: proud to announce Byro has closed €20 in strategic angel funding. after being rejected by YC, Antler, and the TalTech lecture hall wifi, we decided to take destiny into our own hands. the round was heavily oversubscribed by: - grandma (€10 cash, unconditional SAFE) - my technical co-founder finding a €10 bill in his winter jacket. this extends our runway by approximately 3 red bulls. grateful to everyone who believed in the vision when it was just two guys sitting on the floor staring at codex and claude code. big things coming

getting a product to 70% is exciting. getting from 70% to launch is where most founders secretly lose their minds. the first part feels like magic: you sketch workflows, wire up agents, and see the core loop function for the first time. you feel like you're flying. then you hit the remaining stretch, and you realize it is 90% unglamorous friction: hunting down edge cases where an auth token randomly expires. rewriting user drop-off flows because someone clicked back instead of forward. staring at error logs at midnight trying to understand why webhooks failed silently. fixing broken state handling across basic navigation. none of this feels like building the future. it feels like plumbing. building Byro in tallinn at 19, this is the biggest operational difference i've noticed between talking about software and actually shipping it. anyone can build a demo that works in a recorded video. what separates real software from a weekend prototype is having the patience to fix the boring details nobody will ever applaud you for.

started uni in tallinn last week while trying to get Byro from 70% to live. the common advice for young founders is binary: “drop out immediately or you aren't serious.” that advice misses how modern building actually works: 1. dev velocity with cursor and agentic tooling means two people can build what used to take a 6-person engineering team. 2. the bottleneck isn't typing code 14 hours a day anymore. it's distribution, customer discovery, and distribution loops. 3. campus gives you an immediate sandbox of ambitious technical peers you can't replicate sitting alone in a room. the goal isn't playing the dramatic “college dropout” founder role for optics. it's ruthlessly protecting the 4-5 high-focus hours every day where the product gets built.
